name: Hafez al-Assad
summary: Hafez al-Assad took power in a 1970 coup and ruled Syria as an authoritarian presidential system built around the Ba'ath Party, the army and the security services. He held to pan-Arab and anti-Israel positions, allied with the Soviet Union, intervened in Lebanon and crushed the Muslim Brotherhood uprising at Hama in 1982, while later accepting a negotiated peace on a land-for-peace basis.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He built up the army with Soviet aid as a central instrument of his rule.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: He fought the 1973 war to recover occupied land and in his 1980 speech called supporting the occupied territories' resistance a principal national duty.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Article 74 says the budget is not in force unless the People's Assembly approves it.

clerical-rule.rationale: He ran a secular-fronted Ba'ath state and crushed the Islamist uprising against it.

conscription.rationale: Article 40 of the constitution makes military service compulsory, and he built up a large conscript army.

death-penalty.rationale: Law No. 49 (1980) made membership in the Muslim Brotherhood punishable by death, and military field courts handed down death sentences, according to Human Rights Watch.

defeat-communism.rationale: He allied with the Soviet Union and built up his military with Soviet aid.

democracy-best.rationale: He kept a one-party system with single-candidate referendums for 29 years, and scholars describe an authoritarian bargain of security for political quiescence.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He groomed his son Bassel, and after Bassel's death in 1994 his son Bashar, as his successor.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He ruled for three decades under emergency decree, and Human Rights Watch reports the emergency law used to prosecute peaceful expression and to try opponents in state security courts.

foreign-policy-non-interference.rationale: He sent troops into Lebanon in 1976 and kept them there, an occupation that scholars say benefited his security apparatus.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Article 103 of the constitution he promulgated makes the president supreme commander of the army and armed forces; he was also defence minister and a former air force commander.

head-of-state-dissolves-parliament.rationale: Article 107 gives the president power to dissolve the People's Assembly by reasoned decision.

independent-unions.rationale: The constitution assigns popular organisations including unions a role in building and defending the socialist system (Arts. 48-49).

job-guarantee.rationale: Article 36 says the state undertakes to provide work for all citizens.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Article 1 says the Syrian people are part of the Arab nation and work for its comprehensive unity.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: His speeches honour the martyrs who died in the nation's wars and say there is hardly a home in Syria without one.

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: He ordered Syrian forces into Lebanon in 1976 in an operation Britannica and others describe as part of his aim to curb Israel and shape Lebanon, not a defence against attack on Syria.

military-superiority.rationale: He built up the Syrian military with Soviet aid and made it a regional power.

one-party-rule.rationale: The 1973 constitution made the Ba'ath Party the leading party of state and society (Art. 8), with other parties admitted only inside a front it leads; Syria stayed a one-party system throughout his rule.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Under the constitution the president can veto laws and issue legislation himself (Arts. 98, 111), so the People's Assembly was not the supreme lawmaker.

patriotic-education.rationale: Articles 21 and 23 make education nationalist and socialist, aimed at a generation filled with the spirit of struggle for Arab unity, freedom and socialism.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: The constitution names Syria a member of the Union of the Arab Republics (Art. 1), a union of states he joined.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Article 21 aims education at a generation attached to its history and proud of its heritage.

property-fundamental.rationale: Article 14 limits individual ownership by its social function and Article 15 allows expropriation for the public interest with compensation.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Article 14(3) says individual property must not be used against the people's interests and serves the national economy within the development plan.

public-ownership.rationale: The constitution declares a planned socialist economy with public ownership of natural resources and utilities and nationalised enterprises (Arts. 13-14); scholars describe a large public sector under his rule.

recognize-territorial-claims-from-conque.rationale: He demanded that Israel withdraw completely from lands taken in war, and rejected a peace that left them occupied.

return-lost-territory.rationale: In 1980 and again in Geneva in 1994 he demanded complete Israeli withdrawal from occupied Arab land, including the Golan, on the basis of UN resolutions 242 and 338.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The constitution's preamble blames colonial conquest for shattering the Arab nation, and Article 1 commits Syria to work for comprehensive Arab unity.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: He took part in the 1963 and 1966 Ba'ath coups and seized power himself by coup in 1970, which his regime named the corrective revolution.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: His government held no accounting for killings at Hama or executions at Tadmor, and used Hama as a warning to others; Human Rights Watch notes officers responsible kept command or moved on.

separate-church-state.rationale: The constitution requires the president to be Muslim and makes Islamic jurisprudence a main source of legislation (Art. 3), so religion and state were not strictly separate.

separated-powers.rationale: The constitution lets the president legislate by decree (Art. 111), appoint and dismiss all ministers (Art. 95) and hold ministers responsible to him (Art. 117); scholars describe a docile parliament under presidential control.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The constitution makes the economy a planned one run through development plans (Art. 13).

state-harmful.rationale: He built and ran a centralised state apparatus and constitution with the presidency at its centre.

strong-leader.rationale: He replaced collegial Ba'ath decision-making with absolute presidential control and ruled for three decades under emergency powers.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Human Rights Watch documents long detention of political opponents and Tadmor prison abuses, and Law No. 49 made Muslim Brotherhood membership a capital offence; the 1982 Hama assault crushed the Brotherhood uprising.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Article 19 requires taxes on an equitable and progressive basis.

term-limits.rationale: He wrote a constitution without presidential term limits and ruled by repeated referendum until he died in office.

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Article 28 of the constitution bans torture and provides punishment, yet Human Rights Watch documents torture and deaths under torture at Tadmor during his rule: the record points both ways.

traditional-family.rationale: Article 44 calls the family the basic unit of society, protected by the state, which also encourages marriage.

troops-home-from-abroad.rationale: Troops he sent into Lebanon in 1976 stayed there through the rest of his rule.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Article 46 has the state protect citizens' health and provide treatment and medication.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: The constitution sets a seven-year presidential term with no limit on reelection, and he held office from 1971 until his death in 2000.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: He crushed the Islamist uprising against his rule, ending with Hama in 1982.

women-suffrage.rationale: The constitution sets the vote at 18 for citizens without distinction of sex and commits the state to women's full participation in political life (Arts. 45, 54).

notes: Themes searched: government and executive power (constitution, term limits, succession), liberty (emergency law, Tadmor, Hama), society and religion (1980 speech, constitution), economy (constitution, Heydemann), world (Lebanon, Golan, Geneva 1994, Soviet alliance). He wrote no books; the maintainer library and Gutenberg hold none by or on him. Many statements stay null because his texts do not address them.
